comments.author: maerF0x0
comments.textRawHtml:
It strikes me that if their models were good enough for recursive self improvement, then the VCs would have pushed to delay IPO until such time that they had clear market dominance.

For some reason they need the $100B today at the cost of dilution, rather than additional private rounds and/or using cashflow+profits to continue the advancement.

children.author: HarHarVeryFunny
children.textRawHtml:
As has been said many times, this is not a normal IPO meant to raise funds for a growing company. This is a liquidity/exit event to let investors, founders and employees realize paper gains.

It hard to say they are doing this now because they need the money now - they are committed to spending close to $1T ($1000B) on datacenters/etc, and the IPO will only raise them around $50B (5% of what they need).

The timing seems more decided by the fact that growth may never look better than it does now as tokenmaxxing gives way to customers looking for ROI and cheaper alternatives to frontier LLMs, such as decision models and non-frontier LLMs which are rapidly becoming good enough for many use cases.

children.author: kragen
children.textRawHtml:
That claim seems surprising to me, since I'm pretty sure their bonds yield less than 47%.

https://en.sedaily.com/world/2026/10/19/anthropic-offers-10-... says, "According to the Financial Times on Thursday, Blackstone was offered a return of more than 10% on subordinated investment in a $60 billion financing designed to secure Google TPUs for Anthropic [...] The double-digit return is a striking concession given that four months ago Anthropic issued about $4.4 billion of debt at 8.5% in a similar deal known as "Project Big Sky."," so we can estimate 10.5%. 8.5% is already well into junk-bond territory.

Can you explain your calculations?

Their current revenue is US$17 billion per year (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropic) out of the US$128 trillion per year world economy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nomi...). If Anthropic were to continue to grow at 47% per year, they would reach the size of the entire world economy in 02049.

If Anthropic were to have to pay a double-junk-bond-level 15% yield to borrow the 1 trillion [US?] dollars that HarHarVeryFunny says they need, they'd need US$150 billion per year in revenues to service that debt. At 47% growth per year, they would reach that level around Q3 02031. That seems like a relatively unambitious timeline to build out the envisioned trillion dollars' worth of data centers and incur that debt.

children.author: kragen
children.textRawHtml:
I notice you still haven't shared your own calculations.

As to your gloss of my comment, that wasn't what I meant. They would only be losing money until 02031 if they sold one trillion dollars of bonds in the near future, at 15% yield (something like 45% higher than what they're currently paying). This would be an unreasonably bad way for them to fund several years of datacenter construction. In fact, it's roughly the worst possible way. That's why I did that calculation: however bad their actual cash-flow situation is, it won't be that bad.

What they'll presumably actually do is sell those bonds (or additional shares) over the next several years, so that they're never paying interest on money they didn't yet need to borrow.

The interest on US$60 billion at ≈10.5% is only US$6.3 billion per year, which is about a third of their current revenue. Given that they're currently spending US$42 billion per year, this doesn't seem out of proportion.

I agree that nobody has any idea what the AI landscape is going to look like in five years' time. We don't even know if there will be humans.

However, Anthropic's existence as a company is kind of conditioned on explosive growth anyway. If their growth goes into single digits per year, or goes negative, they're dead even if they don't borrow money.

children.author: etempleton
children.textRawHtml:
"However, Anthropic's existence as a company is kind of conditioned on explosive growth anyway. If their growth goes into single digits per year, or goes negative, they're dead even if they don't borrow money."

I agree and this is really my only point. It only works if everything goes according to plan. If it doesn't I think the company fails spectacularly. Not that OpenAI is any different, they are in the same boat, maybe worse off. I don't know if there is any scenario where both can thrive considering their commitments. How much bigger is the addressable market that will pay big to use AI? These are of course questions no one has the answer to, but

Anyway, I have been typing from my phone, so here is my admittedly back of napkin math. Anthropic has $450 billion in near to medium term commitments (through 2030) and another 500 billion after that through 2040 or so, most if not all of which they cannot cancel. So just in per existing commitments they owe already 110 billion+ per year for the next 4 years. I don't know if that is front loaded or back loaded, or evenly spread, but that is the average. That likely does not include all of their costs such as their 3.2 billion annual marketing spend, employee costs, and other annual costs such as their debt servicing which we will put at 6.3 billion per your math, all of which is undoubtedly going to grow. So they need at least 125-150 billion a year minimum for the next four years just to keep the lights on. That is not profit; just break even.

From a revenue growth standpoint they went from 144% QoQ revenue growth in Q2 to 44% QoQ revenue growth Q3. I don't think we can ignore the downward trajectory of their revenue growth. And there are signs that the revenue growth story might get a lot worse in the short term as competition gets more fierce and with companies becoming more discretionary on AI spending meanwhile the cost of computer continues to rise. Short term 15% is probably realistic sustained QoQ growth and after that 5-10% Medium term.

Q1 26 - 5B +132% Q2 26 - 12B +144% Q3 26 - 17B +47% Q4 26 - 20B +20% // Year 26 - 54B Revenue (125B) //

Q1 27 - 23B +15% Q2 27 - 25B +10% Q3 27 - 27B +10% Q4 27 - 30B +10% // Year 27 - 95B Revenue (30B) //

Longer term who knows! Like I said, if they can't keep growing I think think they immediately run into financial and confidence issues and I think the risk of other cheaper models being good enough or OpenAI catching up and surpassing Anthropic is a real risk.

children.author: kragen
children.textRawHtml:
Yeah, if their revenues were US$17 billion a year, and those grow by only 47% per year, that would only add up to US$210 billion of revenues by 02030. But it sounds like you're saying their revenue is growing by 44% per quarter, which would be 330% per year.

https://explodingtopics.com/blog/anthropic-revenue confirms: "Anthropic made $33.2 billion in revenue in the first nine months of 2026, up from $2.5 billion in the same period of 2025 (Anthropic S-1, November 2026) Anthropic’s Q3 2026 revenue was $17.0 billion, up 1,127% from $1.38 billion in Q3 2025 (Anthropic S-1, November 2026)".

It also gives quarterly revenue figures for 02025 (US$0.376B, US$0.787B, US$1.38B, US$2.04B) and for 02026 (US$4.73B, US$11.6B, US$17.0B), all sourced from their S-1/A. Those last two are where we get the 47% revenue growth per quarter, while the Q1 to Q2 growth was 145%.

So evidently I was erring by using quarterly figures not only for growth but also for revenue.

If that growth were to continue, they really would have no trouble at all in paying US$450 billion of expenses. They'd make US$37 trillion dollars between now and 02031, US$11.9 trillion of it in the last quarter of 02030.

This is unlikely to happen, but I really don't think they're about to implode.

In any case, though, I don't think they have US$450 billion of debt currently, and I don't imagine they'll pay for those commitments out of their revenue; I imagine they'll float bonds just like any other business.

children.author: kragen
children.textRawHtml:
It seems unlikely that this exponential growth will continue that long, but it also seems evident that unless AI development hits some kind of technological wall in the next year or two, the US economy in 02030 will look very radically different than it does now, in unpredictable ways.

I think you might be trying to implicitly use historical analogies like the advent of electrical utilities in the late 19th century, or of the internet in the late 20th century. Possibly a closer historical analogy is the arrival of the Spanish in the Aztec Empire in 01519.

In this analogy, we are not the Spaniards.

My calculations above are to understand Anthropic's current and near future financial situation, not to predict a most likely figure for 02030.

children.author: CoolestBeans
children.textRawHtml:
I think this is an overly negative take. The IPO is mostly primary issuance and the cash goes to the company. This extends Anthropic's runway into years rather than months. Crucially, this means revenue growth does not need to reaccelerate and can be allowed to slow to something resembling a healthy technology company.

The IPO has to happen ASAP because financial conditions are deteriorating for Anthropic and private capital has tapped out. They will need cash, they're out of people to get it from, and the cost to get it goes up every day.

I agree the fundamental question of whether Anthropic can grow past its fixed commitments is still a big unanswered question and that there are a lot of fundamental headwinds that you correctly brought up. But at least the IPO takes the business as it exists today seriously.

Crucially, this means revenue growth does not need to reaccelerate and can be allowed to slow to something resembling a healthy technology company.

The IPO has to happen ASAP because financial conditions are deteriorating for Anthropic and private capital has tapped out. They will need cash, they're out of people to get it from, and the cost to get it goes up every day.

I agree the fundamental question of whether Anthropic can grow past its fixed commitments is still a big unanswered question and that there are a lot of fundamental headwinds that you correctly brought up. But at least the IPO takes the business as it exists today seriously.

children.author: jacquesm
children.textRawHtml:
An IPO can be one of two things and it all depends on who knows what: a way to raise cash to fuel future expansion or a way to offload a lot of the risk onto people who have no knowledge about what is really going on behind the official filings. It could be both but that's unlikely and given that this is Anthropic who are already in my 'untrustworthy' book I am betting on the second. There will be something that they can legitimately claim was 'unforeseen' and then maybe the stock will substantially drop past the lock-up period. Unforeseen could range from 'oh look, our growth stagnated, who could have predicted that?' to 'Oh, look, those models we warned you against are eating our lunch' and many others besides.

This is a bubble, the question is whether it will fill out fast enough not to implode, taking earlier bubbles into account I don't think it will, and if it does it will wreck the economy and then it will still implode, only a bit later.

Sketch me a scenario please where they can grow a couple of orders of magnitude and the rest of the economy survives?

The lore is that Ford created the assembly line and paid his people wages high enough that they could afford the product they were making and effectively jumpstarted a massive upgrade in welfare. This is the exact opposite.

children.author: bikvfeee
children.textRawHtml:
> As has been said many times, this is not a normal IPO meant to raise funds for a growing company. This is a liquidity/exit event to let investors, founders and employees realize paper gains.

This has been true for 4-5 decades, not just anthropic. I wonder if the is what Warren buffet had in mind when he came up with his rule of never participating in IPOs.
